text_lr: Text alone carries real signal. The best text-only logistic regression (MiniLM, C = 1) has a three-period selection score of **39.2%**, above the best rule's 34.1%. It is strong on the walk-forward periods (**43.0% / 51.1%**) but weak on val (**23.5%**, below the rule's 28.1%), so it is unstable. Surprisingly the 'stronger' encoder (bge-small) is better on val (38.2%) but worse on the two walk-forward periods, and loses on the selection rule (38.2% vs 39.2%). With 45–121 positives per period these encoder differences are within noise.
text_nn: The small MLP (one hidden layer of 64, lr = 1e-3) is chosen; all six settings fall within 37.5–39.9%. Over 5 seeds its selection score is **39.5% on average, worst seed 38.7%**, barely above the text LR (39.2%). **The refit matters:** training only on the months before the stopping set gives a selection score of **33.9%**, refitting on the full period for the same epoch count gives **39.5%** (+5.6 points). Almost all of the gain is in WF 2023 (**28.3% → 43.0%**), where the stop-set-only net had only 6 months (2022-H1) to learn from. The loss curves show the usual pattern: training loss keeps falling while the stopping-set loss bottoms out after 5–13 epochs.
combined: Adding text to the tabular model does **not** beat gradient boosting alone on the selection rule. (a) The tabular+text network: **44.8%** (5-seed mean, worst seed 42.6%), and the refit again helps a lot (37.3% → 44.8%). (b) Gradient boosting + out-of-fold text score: **45.3%**. (c) Late fusion of gradient boosting and the text MLP: **46.7%**. All are close to gradient boosting alone (**47.4%**). The combinations change *where* the model is good: late fusion has the best worst period (**42.6%** vs 39.7%) and WF 2023 (46.3% vs 39.7%), but it gives up val (42.6% vs 47.1%).
ci: On val at K = 110 no text-based model beats gradient boosting alone: the best are (b) and (c) at **42.6%**, −4.4 and −5.1 points vs gradient boosting (P(better) 18–19%). Both still clearly beat the best rule (**+15.5 points [+2.6, +29.2], P = 99%** for (b); +14.8, P = 97% for (c)). Text-only models are not reliably better than the rule at K = 110 (text MLP +3.7, P = 64%; text LR −3.6, P = 27%). At **K = 305** the picture flips: the tabular+text network catches **75.0%** [63–84], the highest of all models, vs 67.6% for gradient boosting.
curve: Gradient boosting leads at small capacity (≤ 150/month). Above ~200/month the tabular+text network pulls ahead and stays on top up to 600/month (≈ 88% recall at 575). The text-only curves sit between the rules and the tabular models. So the description adds information that matters **after** the most obvious candidates (known-exploited vendors, critical network bugs) are already patched.
sensitivity: Edits do **not** inflate the text models. On the 919-CVE history sample, scores from today's description and from the reconstructed earliest description agree closely (Spearman **0.977**; **0.936** on the 171 edited CVEs). Val recall@110 actually goes **up** slightly with the earliest text: text LR 23.5% → 26.5%, gradient boosting + text 42.6% → 45.6% (+2 CVEs each). Re-encoding on CPU reproduces the stored GPU embeddings exactly (mean cosine 1.0000). So training on today's `description_day0` is fine; we note it as a checked limitation (history covers only the sample + phrase CVEs).
final: Under the selection rule **gradient boosting on tabular features (05a) remains the best model: 47.4%** three-period mean, 47.1% val recall@110. Late fusion with the text MLP is a close second (**46.7%**) with a **better worst period (42.6% vs 39.7%)**, and the tabular+text network is best at large capacity (**75.0% at K = 305**). Text alone reaches ~39%, above the best rule (34.1%) but unstable. The description's information overlaps heavily with vendor/CNA/CVSS, and frozen general-purpose sentence embeddings add little at K = 110. A model fine-tuned on CVE language (Step 6c) is the next test.
